authorities_checked.exact_section: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19(d): prescribing and dispensing an opioid antagonist to a person at risk or a family member, friend or other person in a position to assist; legitimate-medical-purpose clause for chapters 94C and 112

M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19A(a)-(g): emergency contraception definition; department shall ensure and Commissioner or designated physician shall issue the statewide standing order; pharmacist may dispense; permissive training and its required content in (d); annual count report, no patient identification, confidential, not public records under clause Twenty-sixth of G.L. c. 4, s. 7 or G.L. c. 66, s. 10 in (e); no aggregate-report provision

M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19B(a)-(h): opioid antagonist definition; department shall ensure, Commissioner or designated physician may issue, order shall include written standardized procedures or protocols; (c) pharmacist may dispense and good-faith protection except gross negligence or willful misconduct; (d) annual dose report, no patient identification, confidential, not a public record, department aggregate report; (e) purchaser billing for dispensing pursuant to s. 19B, reasonable effort to submit claim prior to dispensing unless purchaser requests out-of-pocket; (f) issuer and practitioner protection; (g) good-faith receipt, possession, administration and immunity, s. 34A immunity

M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19C: Board shall promulgate continuous-supply regulations for pharmacies in areas with high incidence of opiate overdose as determined by the Board in consultation with the department; provisos that the continuous supply shall include FDA-approved over-the-counter opioid antagonists and that such pharmacies shall notify the department of insufficient supply or stock

M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19E(a)-(g): COVID-19 control measure definition; Commissioner or designated actively practicing physician may issue a standing order; protocols consistent with the July 6, 2022 revised Paxlovid EUA and PREP Act declarations; (c) mandatory training before dispensing a COVID-19 drug; (d) report upon request on doses, tests or devices, confidential, not a public record, aggregate annual report, no patient-identification sentence; (e) and (f) noted as outside the section's declared scope

M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1: definitions of "Dispense" (delivery of a controlled substance by a practitioner or pursuant to the order of a practitioner) and "Practitioner" (paragraphs (a) and (b)), incorporated by the 247 CMR 2.00 definition of Dispensing

M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18D(a)-(b) (duty on dispensing a Schedule II opioid to inform of risks and offer an opioid antagonist), and the section captions of s. 19F, s. 21 (pamphlet paragraph read) and s. 34A, checked for the section's cross-references
M.G.L. c. 94C section index, ss. 18-21: confirms ss. 19A, 19B and 19E are the pharmacist standing-order regimes; ss. 19B1/2 and 19D1/2 are separate mechanisms

247 CMR 9.06(1)(a)-(d), (2)(a)-(b), (3), (4) and (5) (page footer 12/6/24): high overdose area, pamphlet and opioid antagonist definitions; continuous supply in a high overdose area; dispensing by a pharmacy not in such an area; counseling and pamphlet at the time of dispensing; referral to nearest location; rescue kit outer-package label and expiration date
247 CMR 2.00, definition of Dispensing (delivery to an ultimate user pursuant to the lawful order of a practitioner as defined in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1)

105 CMR 700.000 current edition (Mass. Register #1514, 2/2/2024; 39 pages): 700.001 definition of Prescription Drug (federal prescription legend); 700.003(F), (F)(1)(a)-(c) and (F)(2)(a)-(b); 700.004(B)(6), (B)(7), (B)(11) and (B)(13)

results.summary: KEEP. I checked every field of the section (orientation, all four comparison tables cell by cell, five worked examples, 35 retrieval prompts and answers, quick review, decision logic, ma_vs_federal, exceptions, timing, forms, role duties, traps and drug examples) against the current official texts and found no proposition that misstates Massachusetts law or would mislead a candidate. Standing orders: the section keeps the three chapter 94C regimes apart correctly. The department shall ensure an order under s. 19A(b) and s. 19B(b); the Commissioner or designated physician shall issue the emergency contraception order but may issue the opioid antagonist order, and the Commissioner or an actively practicing designated physician may issue the s. 19E(b) order, whose protocols must follow the July 6, 2022 revised Paxlovid EUA and PREP Act declarations. Training is permissive in s. 19A(d), mandatory in s. 19E(c) only before dispensing a COVID-19 drug, and absent from s. 19B and 247 CMR 9.06. Reporting is annual in s. 19A(e) and s. 19B(d) and upon request in s. 19E(d); the no-patient-identification sentence appears only in s. 19A(e) and s. 19B(d); all three reports are confidential and outside the public-records definition; only s. 19B(d) and s. 19E(d) provide an aggregate department report. Nothing from one regime leaks into another. Opioid antagonists: s. 19(d), s. 19B(a)-(g) and 247 CMR 9.06(1)-(5) are paraphrased faithfully, including the gross negligence and willful misconduct exception in s. 19B(c) and (f) and its absence from s. 19B(g). The s. 19B(e) purchaser-billing rule is consistently confined to dispensing pursuant to s. 19B, with the reasonable-effort claim before dispensing and the out-of-pocket exception. On stocking, the section states the location trigger in 247 CMR 9.06(1)(a) and (2)(a)-(b), then Policy 2024-01's statement (Adopted 1/11/24, Revised 2/6/25; no later revision is listed) that all areas of Massachusetts experience high incidences of opioid-related overdoses or deaths so Massachusetts pharmacies are required to stock naloxone under s. 19C and keep a continuous, sufficient supply. It flags the policy as guidance rather than a list of areas and recommends a continuous supply in every Massachusetts pharmacy. That matches retail inspection item 60 and the July 13, 2026 standing order's reference to the policy. The two s. 19C provisos (over-the-counter antagonists in the supply; notice to the department of insufficient supply or stock) are quoted accurately. The policy's reporting method (daily PMP submissions preferred, data-collection only; otherwise an emailed report by January 15 for the previous calendar year with pharmacy name and zip code, total doses rather than prescriptions or manufacturer units, and doses paid by insurance; per-event details encouraged, not required) is exact. Over-the-counter naloxone: the packaging test, the statement that the Drug Control Program's regulations do not apply, and the statement that no MCSR is required track the October 10, 2024 advisory. The packaging legend matches the 105 CMR 700.001 definition of Prescription Drug. The conclusion that an ordinary over-the-counter sale is not dispensing under 247 CMR 2.00 (which requires delivery pursuant to the lawful order of a practitioner), so 247 CMR 9.06(3) counseling and the pamphlet are not engaged, is sound. It is conditioned on a sale made without a prescription or the standing order, so it leaves the duties in place whenever naloxone is dispensed on either. The DPH 12/20/2023 memorandum's 'should' is kept as guidance. 105 CMR 700.004(B)(11) is quoted exactly, including 'approved by the Department'. Emergency vaccines: 105 CMR 700.003(F) (2/2/2024 edition) is reproduced accurately: the Commissioner's designation, insufficiency determination and order, administration under both the Commissioner's order and a practitioner's order or prescription, the student's authorization and supervision condition, the (F)(2) training, supervision and protocol subjects for every person administering, and the (B)(7) registration exemption. All seven practice questions (MA-Q-0097, 0098, 0318, 0325, 0348, 0349, 0350) can be answered from the section, and neither their keys nor their explanations are contradicted by it. Scope notes, not defects: s. 19E(e) purchaser billing, the protections in s. 19A(c) and (f) and s. 19E(f), Policy 2024-01's section I guidance beyond what 247 CMR 9.06 itself requires (the Schedule II offer, the purchaser-insurance steps, 'Naloxone Rescue Kit' in place of name and address, the list of acceptable pamphlets, signage) and its section III on remote locations all exist but fall outside the scope the section declares, and nothing in the section suggests they are absent.
